So Shadowscale-tier? Alright then. I'll mostly go over armour and accessories as other people seem to have got the weapons covered.

**Crimson Armour** which you would have gotten from the Brain is especially useful - while the 6% increased damage (to all types) seems a bit lacking, Crimson Armour's true strength lies in its set bonus, which increases your health regeneration speed by 50%. This is incredibly useful for basically the rest of Normalmode, and maybe even early Hardmode before you make yourself a new set of armour. If you're willing to world-hop, you can also get **Shadowscale Armour** from a Corruption world, which increases Melee attack speed and movement speed. It's not quite as good as Crimson's regen buff, but it's good for Melee builds if you don't need the regen.

If you plan on specialising in Magic weapons, there's also **Meteor Armour** which is pretty great if you plan on using magic weapons - a full set of Meteor Armour increases the damage of magic weapons by 21%, as well as making the Space Gun weapon require 0 Mana to fire. It's a really good combo, and arguably slightly overpowered for where in the game you get it. **Jungle Armour** is also pretty good for magic, sacrificing some damage for extra Mana and reduced Mana usage on all weapons, as well as having a little extra defence compared to Meteor.

As for accessories, you should have Hermes Boots and maybe a Cloud by now. If not, dive into the Underground Desert and grab some! If you've encountered a Goblin Army, you should encounter the Goblin Tinkerer underground, who will move into your town. He sells both Rocket Boots and the Tinkerer's Table, both being incredibly useful items. Rocket Boots basically give you a second of flat-out *flight,* while the Tinkerer's Table lets you combine similar accessories into one. (For example, Hermes Boots and Rocket Boots can be combined into Spectre Boots, having the bonuses of both.)

As for other accessories, I'll make a list of some early usefuls:

* **Spectre Boots** I'll mention again, because they're essential. A second of flight plus the speed of Hermes Boots. They're so good.
* **Celestial Cuffs** are fantastic for Magic builds. They increase the pickup range of mana stars (Celestial Magnet, sold by the Travelling Merch) while also recovering Mana from any damage you take (Magic Cuffs, from a Mana Regen Band and a Shackle) - note that you'll need to break Shadow Orbs in a Corruption world to get the Band of Starpower to make the Mana Regen Band.
* **Feral Claws** are great for Melee builds. Acquired from the Underground Jungle, they increase your Melee attack speed by 12%.
* **Obsidian Shield** is a combination of the Cobalt Shield (from the Dungeon) and an Obsidian Skull (crafted). It allows you to stand on hot blocks (like Hellstone and Meteorite) as well as resisting knockback from attacks. You also get a free +2 defence.
* Weirdly enough, a **Shackle** is surprisingly useful early on, if only because of its drop rate. Because it drops so commonly, chances are you're going to get one with a really good modifier. A Warding Shackle is a whopping *+5* Defence, which is really good early on. The shackle itself isn't great, but it's the easiest accessory to get a good modifier on.
* A **Lava Charm** is especially useful, but also very rare. Found near the lava layer in the Caverns, it allows you to harmlessly swim in lava for up to 7 seconds. Very useful when mining in dangerous places.

If you're playing in Expert Mode, you'll also have access to:

* The **Shield of Cthulhu**, which is absolutely essential to any build. Expert Bosses are fast, so you need to move faster.
* The **Hive Pack** makes some of your bees better, which is great for any build except Melee. The Bee's Knees (Ranged), the Bee Gun (Magic) and Beenades (Throwing) all benefit from this. The Beekeeper (Melee) also benefits, but it's not a very good weapon.

As for your other accessory slots... it's mostly down to your playstyle. You're probably still at the "get what you're dealt with" stage at this point, so keep exploring underground to find new accessories.

If you're under 50% Fishing Power (or if you're fishing in a pool under 300 tiles big), you have a chance to catch junk *instead* of what you'd normally catch. Ideally, you'd want to have 50+ Fishing Power in a lake 300+ tiles big. (The Fisherman's Pocket Guide accessory will tell you if you're fishing in a lake which is too small.)

Your total Fishing Power is a combination of your Fishing Power and your Bait Power. There are also modifiers which can affect your total Fishing Power, like the moon phase, time of day, lake size or if it's raining. The more total Fishing Power you have, the better chance you have to catch rarer items *and* the faster you'll get a fish to bite your hook. (Though the speed at which fish will bite caps out at 125% total Fishing Power, you'll still get rarer fish or crates by increasing your total Fishing Power further.)

Note that the chance of catching a crate never changes - it's always 10%, unless you're below 50% total Fishing Power (catching junk instead). The *rarity* of the crate is what changes with your total Fishing Power, with better Power being able to get better crates (with more items inside them, obviously - if you're fishing for ores, iron crates will have many more bars in them than wooden crates, as an example). You can double your chance of catching crates to 20% with a Crate Potion.

Some other tips I have:

* Try to fight monsters one-at-a-time. If there's a lot of monsters in a room, hang by the entrance and bait the ones which move at you out, so you don't have to deal with them all at once.
* Your shovel is an essential tool. If you stand still for a beat, you'll lose your coin multiplier - however, you don't lose that multiplier if you stand still by *performing an action* - and one of the easiest actions to perform for the purpose of standing still is *digging a wall.* If you know a monster will attack you if you move towards it on the next beat, just wait for a beat and bait it into coming to you instead.
* When dealing with Red Dragons, you can bait out the fireball attack by simply attacking them horizontally immediately after they've moved. This is done in an identical manner to the Lynel Dance from CoH, but unlike Lynels, Red Dragons do not fireball up or down - only horizontally.
* A torch's strength also determines its aggro range. With no torch (or a Level 1 torch), your aggro range is fairly small. With a Luminous Torch, you'll aggro everything you see. Sometimes, the ability to see through walls just isn't worth it... (And this is why I'd say the Torch of Walls is the best torch in the game, unless you have a map. Torch of Walls is a DLC item, but the Switch version has the DLC as standard.)
* Don't underestimate the power of 3 damage! You can break crates and barrels just by attacking them if you deal 3 or more damage with your primary weapon. Obsidian weapons deal 3 damage with a full coin multiplier, Glass weapons deal *4* damage but break if you take damage.
* If you're playing Single Zones (normal) mode, focus on unlocking NPCs above all else - any NPC you find will be *permanently* added to the lobby, and they often have very helpful features like allowing you to practice fighting against monsters/bosses, or removing items from the Single Zones item pool. (Nothing affects All Zones mode.)
* Zone 3 is a killer and will try to overwhelm you by giving you enemies from each direction. Do not be disheartened - deal with the monsters coming at you immediately (without aggroing more), then slowly make you way through the zone. If you're playing Z3 in Single Zones mode, I hope you have the Diamond Dealer unlocked - because it's brutal with the starting dagger. (I find Z3 may actually be easier to clear in All Zones Mode because of this.)
* Unlike Cadence of Hyrule, you can't quick-switch weapons on the fly. (Unless you have a holster, anyway.) Due to this, Glass weapons aren't quite as useful - as you're forced to stick with them until you find something else or they break. If a glass weapon breaks, you will drop a glass shard *at your feet*, which acts identically as the base, 1-damage dagger. However, you need to find the time to pick the shard up... (Though for all these downsides, glass weapons are *more powerful* than they are in CoH - dealing 4 damage instead of 3.)
* *Shrines* can be dangerous, but also beneficial. They often have both beneficial and detrimental effects when activated. Each shrine also drops an item if you blow it up with a bomb, and the item is *usually* the same every time (depending on the shrine). Note that the item will be different depending on if the shrine has been activated or not. (As an example, the Boss Shrine - the one with two skulls on it - drops Cheese if you blow it up. If you blow it up after activating it, it drops a Strength Charm instead. Activating it will also give you one of three random items, but future floors will spawn *two* minibosses instead of one.)

I'll admit though, the game does an absolutely *terrible* job of explaining the modes. I'll give a better explanation:

Character Modes:

* **Journey** - "Creative Mode" character. Can only be used on worlds in Journey Mode.
* **Classic** - Standard mode of play. Drop only money on death, though the amount you drop depends on your World Mode.
* **Mediumcore** - Drop all your items on death. Often referred to as "Tediumcore" or "Hardcore Minus" by fans of the game, because there's often no real way of getting your items back. *Only for those who want to feel pain.*
* **Hardcore** - Once you die, you're dead for good. *Only for those who want to feel pain.*

World Modes: (ie: The actual difficulty mode you were looking for)

* **Journey** - "Creative Mode" world, though Terraria's rules are a bit different. Items have to be encountered first in Journey Mode before they can be duplicated, and you can choose how difficult you want the game to be on-the-fly.
* **Classic** - Standard difficulty recommended for new players.
* **Expert Mode** - Hard difficulty recommended for experienced players. Enemy HP and damage is doubled, and some enemies have new AI. ***(Probably what you were looking for.)***
* **Master Mode** - Extreme difficulty recommended for true masters of the game. Enemy HP and damage is tripled, but there are no AI differences compared to Expert. Prepare to die a lot.
* (Special Mention: The "For The Worthy" World Seed, which can be *stacked* with existing world modes to further increase the difficulty. Many people prefer FTW in Expert Mode compared to Master Mode itself.)

All Mediumcore and Hardcore does is just increase the punishment for death. They do *nothing* to actually affect the difficulty of the game, they only serve to increase tedium.
